blocks.content: A mutex, short for mutual exclusion lock, is a lock that lets only one thread touch a piece of shared data at a time. It is the most common tool for fixing the race conditions that plague multithreaded programs. This chapter covers exactly how a mutex works, why waiting threads sleep instead of spin, and the mistakes that turn a simple lock into a deadlock.

A mutex builds directly on the critical section problem: some section of code touches shared data and must run in isolation from every other thread. A spinlock protects that section by busy waiting, while a mutex protects it by putting waiting threads to sleep. This chapter covers the mutex object itself, its usage pattern, ownership rules, and the traps that cause real bugs.
1. What Is a Mutex

A mutex is a synchronization object with exactly two states: LOCKED and UNLOCKED. It exposes two core operations, acquire (also called lock) and release (also called unlock). At any moment at most one thread can hold the lock; every other thread that wants it must wait its turn.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: A mutex is a lock with two states and two operations that guarantees only one thread is ever inside the protected section.
2. Basic Usage: Lock, Critical Section, Unlock
blocks.text: 2. Basic Usage: Lock, Critical Section, Unlock

blocks.content: Using a mutex follows one fixed pattern. A thread calls lock() before touching the shared data, does its work inside what is now a safe critical section, then calls unlock() to let others in. If no other thread holds the lock, all of this happens instantly.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408416806-713508105.png
blocks.alt: Basic Usage: Lock, Critical Section, Unlock

blocks.content: 3. When the Lock Is Already Taken
blocks.text: 3. When the Lock Is Already Taken

blocks.content: If a second thread calls lock() while the mutex is already LOCKED, it does not get the lock immediately. The operating system blocks that thread, removing it from the processor entirely so it burns no CPU while it waits. This sleeping behavior is the defining trait of a mutex.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408416806-983759602.png
blocks.alt: When the Lock Is Already Taken

blocks.content: When the owning thread calls unlock(), the operating system wakes a waiting thread and lets it acquire the lock. This is different from a spinlock, which keeps checking the lock in a tight loop instead of sleeping. The sibling Spinlock topic covers that busy waiting approach in full.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408416806-176611945.png
blocks.alt: When the Lock Is Already Taken

5. Ownership: Only the Owner May Unlock
blocks.text: 5. Ownership: Only the Owner May Unlock

blocks.content: A mutex is owned by whichever thread successfully locked it. In almost every implementation, only that same thread may call unlock(); any other thread that tries gets an error or undefined behavior.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408416806-727749109.png
blocks.alt: Ownership: Only the Owner May Unlock

blocks.title: Mutex versus semaphore
blocks.content: Ownership is what separates a mutex from a semaphore. A semaphore has no owner, so any thread can signal it regardless of which thread waited. The sibling Semaphore topic explores that contrast fully.
6. The Danger of Deadlock
Mutexes remove races but introduce a new risk: deadlock. The classic case is two threads that each hold one mutex and then wait forever for the other thread's mutex, so neither ever proceeds.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408416806-473576417.png

blocks.title: Full topic ahead
blocks.content: This circular wait is just one deadlock pattern. Detecting, preventing, and recovering from deadlocks gets an entire module of its own; this is only the seed.
7. Mutex in Real Code

Most languages and libraries expose a mutex with the same three operations under different names. The POSIX threads library uses pthread_mutex_lock and pthread_mutex_unlock, and nearly every implementation follows the same init, lock, unlock, destroy shape.
8. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle
blocks.text: 8. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle

blocks.content: The single most common mutex bug is forgetting to unlock on every exit path. If a function locks a mutex and then returns early on an error, or an exception skips past unlock(), every other thread that calls lock() on that mutex blocks forever.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408416992-590625921.png
blocks.alt: Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle

blocks.content: The second common bug is calling lock() twice on the same mutex from the same thread. A plain mutex is not reentrant, so the second lock() call blocks waiting for a lock the thread itself already holds, an instant self deadlock. Only a reentrant, or recursive, mutex allows this safely, by tracking a lock count instead of a single owner.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408416992-19616594.png

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Interviewers often ask you to spot the bug in a locking snippet, explain why a mutex blocks instead of spins, or justify choosing a mutex over a semaphore. Being able to draw the lock and unlock states from memory, and to name ownership as the defining mutex property, covers most of what gets asked.
